# Introduction to Act 3

In Act 3, the characters travel to Perivale St. Andrews, the idyllic company town built around Andrew Undershaft's munitions factory. Here, Shaw contrasts the harsh poverty of the Salvation Army shelter in Act 2 with the clean, prosperous, but morally complex environment of the weapons manufacturer. 

The play reaches its climax as Barbara and her fiancé, Adolphus Cusins, grapple with Undershaft's philosophy: that poverty is a crime and that material wealth and power (even if derived from weapons) are prerequisites for spiritual salvation.

---

# Act 3

*(The library in Lady Britomart's house. It is the following day. Barbara is sitting on the settee, reading. Cusins is at the window. Sarah is on the settee. Charles Lomax is in the armchair.)*

**LADY BRITOMART.** Nobody can tell me anything. Here we are, all waiting for your father, and not one of us knows what we are waiting for.

**LOMAX.** He said something about taking us all over the works [**The works**: *The factory where Undershaft manufactures munitions and cannons.*]{.aside}, didn't he?

**LADY BRITOMART.** And why are we to be taken over the works? What are we to do there?

**LOMAX.** Well, I suppose we shall see how the things are made.

**LADY BRITOMART.** What things?

**LOMAX.** Oh, cannons and torpedoes and things.

**LADY BRITOMART.** Charles Lomax: if you cannot be serious, you had better go away. We are going to Perivale St Andrews to settle about Barbara's future. 

**LOMAX.** I say! Are we? What about my future?

**LADY BRITOMART.** Your future is settled, Charles. You are going to be a millionaire at thirty-five. Until then you are going to be a nuisance.

**LOMAX.** Oh, I say!

*(Undershaft comes in.)*

**UNDERSHAFT.** Good morning, my dear. Good morning, Sarah. Good morning, Barbara. Good morning, Charles. Good morning, Adolphus.

**LADY BRITOMART.** You are late, Andrew.

**UNDERSHAFT.** I am sorry, my dear. I have had a busy morning.

**LADY BRITOMART.** I suppose you have been making more cannons.

**UNDERSHAFT.** No: I have been selling them. To the Japanese, my dear.

**LADY BRITOMART.** And what do they want with cannons?

**UNDERSHAFT.** To shoot the Russians, my dear. [**To shoot the Russians**: *A reference to the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905), which was contemporaneous with the writing of the play.*]{.aside}

**LADY BRITOMART.** Really, Andrew, I do think you might find some more respectable occupation.

**UNDERSHAFT.** My dear: it is the most respectable occupation in the world. It is the only one that pays.

**LADY BRITOMART.** Nonsense! There are plenty of other things that pay.

**UNDERSHAFT.** Not so well, my dear. And not so surely. Look at me. I am a millionaire. I am a power in Europe. I can dictate to governments. I can make war and prevent war. I can buy the press. I can buy the church. I can buy the politicians. And all because I make cannons.

**LADY BRITOMART.** It is very wicked.

**UNDERSHAFT.** It is very profitable. And it is the foundation of our entire civilization. Without cannons, there would be no peace, no order, no law, no government, no property, no religion, no nothing. The man who makes cannons is the true savior of society.

**BARBARA** *(who has been listening in silence)* And the true savior of souls, papa?

**UNDERSHAFT.** Yes, my dear. The true savior of souls. Because poverty is a crime. [**Poverty is a crime**: *Shaw's central thesis in the play, asserting that poverty forces people into immorality and degradation, and that eliminating it is a moral imperative.*]{.aside} It is the worst of crimes. It is the mother of all crimes. And I, by providing employment and good wages and clean homes and healthy food and good clothes, am saving more souls than all your Salvation Army shelters put together.
